extracted.intended_audience: authors seeking literary representation / writers preparing query letters and submission packages
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting and sending a query letter and submission package to a literary agency (specifically Trident Media Group) — covering what to include, tone, comps, bios, follow-up, and what to avoid. Useful for fiction and non-fiction writers seeking representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Your query should be professional, informative, concise, and eye-catching
rubrics_metrics.description: Your pitch is your golden opportunity to present yourself, and your work, to a literary agent; the ideal query is professional, informative, concise, and, most importantly, eye-catching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-written query can be the difference between further conversation and a pass. Make it count: present the project and yourself clearly and engagingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open with the basics
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the literary agent about the meat and potatoes of your project right off the bat — include the title, genre, and word count within only a paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume such information is implied or leave it to the end; be clear and upfront. Example: “I’m pleased to send you for consideration my debut literary novel, ULYSSES, which comes in at 90,000 words.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft an eye-catching logline
rubrics_metrics.description: Write one strong sentence that grabs (or, hooks!) the reader’s attention while capturing what the book is about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may be the most difficult and possibly the most important element — agents often look here first when sifting through queries. Aim for a single, compelling sentence that encapsulates the premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a brief plot synopsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide one or two paragraphs following the logline that give more detail about the plot and the characters, or the subject matter of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep it short and focused; it can help to read descriptive copy on book flaps or back covers for inspiration. Do not include lengthy synopses unless explicitly requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose strong ‘comp’ titles
rubrics_metrics.description: List comparative titles (‘comps’) to help agents and editors orient your work in the market and understand how it can fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List at least one title in the same genre published within the last five years. You can frame projects as X meets Y or for fans of X and Y. Movies/TV/plays may be listed as supplementary comps but should not replace books (do not list only non-book comps). Give comps that accurately place your book on the shelf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the most of your author bio
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide clear, specific information about your publishing history, prizes, education, work experience, social media presence, and whether you are a debut author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you’ve published before, include publisher names and, if possible, sales figures. If you’ve won or been nominated for competitions, be exact. Mention self-published work and link to public social accounts (Twitter, Instagram, Facebook) if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nail the tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the query letter to get a bit of your written voice across while respecting the conventional query format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don’t need to reinvent the wheel stylistically — clarity and concision demonstrate your ability to summarise and pitch, which in itself reflects writing skill. Balance showing voice with following expected query structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flaunt your connections
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have endorsements, blurbs, or potential endorsements from bestselling or award-winning authors, include them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author endorsements and blurbs strengthen a submission; list any collected blurbs or potential endorsers where relevant. Also consider using comp titles as part of demonstrating connections/market placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do your research (send to the right agent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure you’re sending to the agent who’s the right fit for your project and explain why your project fits their interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual agents often specialise in particular genres/age ranges even within a large agency. Check agents’ profiles, Publisher’s Marketplace, and social media to see what they currently represent. It’s okay to mention titles they represent as comps or evidence of fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when (and when not) to follow up
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that agents receive many queries and may not be able to reply to every letter; follow-up etiquette is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agent requests material, it’s acceptable to check in if you haven’t heard back after a month. Always notify an agent if you’ve received an offer of representation from another agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of what not to do
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not violate or work outside submission rules; avoid including unsolicited lengthy synopses, excerpts, full manuscripts, or attachments; avoid cold calling or sending physical materials unless requested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking stated submission rules will not make you stand out positively and may prevent an agent from reading your query at all. Most agencies also ask that you do not call them to cold query or follow up, and that you do not send physical materials via the mail.
